content.title: Space Weather | DeSoto County. FL
content.text: NOAA Space Weather Monitoring DashboardPresenting Real-Time Data for Infrastructure Protection and Operational AwarenessMission Statement: Space weather refers to conditions originating from the Sun and in the space environment that can adversely affect technology and critical infrastructure on Earth and in orbit. Severe events pose risks to power grids, satellite operations, Global Positioning Systems (GPS), and radio communications—all essential for mission continuity and emergency response.Usage Guidelines: All data visualizations are loaded in real-time directly from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC). This embedded dashboard requires a manual refresh to display the absolute latest data.Overall Space Weather Status (3-Day History)Operational Impact Summary:Solar Flares (Top Panel): Rapid spikes (M or X-class) indicate an immediate and severe risk of High-Frequency (HF) radio communication blackouts on the sunlit side of Earth.Proton Flux (Middle Panel): Elevated levels signify a Solar Radiation Storm (S-Scale event), which threatens satellite electronics, degrades sensitive GPS signals, and poses radiation exposure risks to polar aviation.Geomagnetic Activity (Bottom Panel): High Kp-index values (red/yellow) denote a Geomagnetic Storm (G-Scale event). This requires preparation for potential regional power grid disturbances and wide-area GPS system degradation.Solar Wind & Interplanetary Magnetic Field (IMF)ACE Magnetometer & Solar Wind (3-Day)Solar Wind Speed (7-Day)Operational Impact Summary:The Interplanetary Magnetic Field (IMF) and Solar Wind Velocity are primary drivers of geomagnetic storms.Bz Component (Middle Panel): A strong, persistent southward orientation (negative Bz) is the most critical factor for initiating a major geomagnetic storm capable of inducing geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) in power grids and pipelines.Solar Wind Speed: High speeds (above 500 km/s) increase the severity of storm impacts. Sudden increases indicate the imminent arrival of coronal mass ejections (CMEs).Radio Communication Disruption (D-RAP Model)D-Region Absorption - Global ViewD-RAP - North Pole ViewCRITICAL Operational Impact:The D-RAP model indicates the predicted severity of High-Frequency (HF) radio absorption due to solar X-ray flares.Red/Orange Regions: Areas experiencing significant radio blackout (R-Scale events) are colored here.Impact: Blackouts immediately affect long-range air-to-ground communications, military and maritime communications, and emergency/amateur radio backup systems that rely on the ionosphere.Action: Personnel relying on HF communications should monitor this map and be prepared to switch to alternate communication methods or Very High Frequency (VHF) links.Aurora and Geomagnetic Activity ForecastsAurora Forecast (Northern Hemisphere)Aurora Forecast (Southern Hemisphere)Operational Impact Summary:The expansion of the auroral oval is a direct consequence of a geomagnetic storm.Low-Latitude Aurora: When the aurora is forecast to be visible at low latitudes (south of 50° N/S), it signifies a severe G3-G5 geomagnetic storm.Impact: These severe storms carry the greatest risk for power grid infrastructure due to Geomagnetically Induced Currents (GICs). They also cause prolonged and severe GPS/GNSS signal degradation and potential satellite orbit drag issues.Action: Infrastructure and power utility partners should be notified when the forecast indicates a significant expansion of the auroral zone.Proton Flux & Solar Radiation StormsEnergetic Proton Flux Levels (Solar Radiation Storm Indicator)View Full SizeOperational Impact Summary:Elevated proton flux levels are an indicator of a Solar Radiation Storm (S-Scale event).Impact on Satellites: High-energy protons can penetrate spacecraft shielding, causing Single Event Upsets (SEUs) in satellite electronics and potentially damaging solar panels. This can disrupt emergency satellite communications and weather sensing capabilities.Impact on Aviation: Radiation storms pose a health risk to passengers and crew on high-altitude, polar air routes. Aviation partners should monitor the S-scale for potential route diversions.Additional Resources and Scale ExplanationsNOAA Space Weather ScalesThese scales classify the severity of space weather events (Level 1 to 5).R-Scale: Radio Blackouts (R1-R5) - Impact on HF Comms.S-Scale: Solar Radiation Storms (S1-S5) - Impact on Satellites & Aviation.G-Scale: Geomagnetic Storms (G1-G5) - Impact on Power Grids & GPS.View Detailed Scale Explanations
